definition: A break of the radius, ulna, or both, often after a fall on an outstretched hand, causing pain, swelling, and deformity between the elbow and wrist.
A fatal encephalitis classically linked to a bite from an infected mammal, with hydrophobia and aerophobia.
An acute unilateral lower motor neuron facial palsy causing weakness of the entire side of the face.
A red, swollen tongue with prominent papillae, classically seen in scarlet fever and Kawasaki disease.
A cat-associated infection classically causing regional lymphadenopathy after an inoculation papule.
A varicella-zoster infection causing crops of itchy vesicles in different stages of healing.
An X-linked coagulation disorder caused by factor IX deficiency, producing deep bleeding and hemarthroses.
Inability to dorsiflex the ankle, typically from common peroneal nerve or L5 root injury, so the toes catch on the ground when walking.
A metabolic disorder characterized by chronic hyperglycemia from inadequate insulin secretion, action, or both.
A cold injury producing numb, pale or waxy skin that can become blistered or necrotic after rewarming.
A radiographic deformity in which one bone end is eroded to a point and the adjacent bone base is cupped, classically seen in psoriatic arthritis.
Hard deposits of cholesterol or bilirubin in the biliary tract that can cause episodic right upper quadrant pain, especially after fatty meals.
A herpesvirus infection producing grouped painful vesicles, often recurring at the oral or genital sites.
A finger deformity from rupture or avulsion of the extensor tendon at the distal phalanx, leaving the fingertip unable to actively extend.
A neurodevelopmental disorder with severe speech impairment, ataxia, happy demeanor, and frequent inappropriate laughter.
A superficial dermatophyte infection of the feet causing interdigital scaling, itching, and fissuring.
A radiographic finding of two gas-filled chambers in the upper abdomen, classically indicating duodenal atresia in newborns.
A fluid-filled swelling in the popliteal fossa, often arising from a knee joint effusion.
An intestinal nematode infection acquired through skin penetration, classically associated with barefoot exposure to contaminated soil.
A nasal deformity with a collapsed, depressed bridge, seen after trauma, cocaine use, granulomatosis with polyangiitis, or congenital syphilis.
A sympathetic pathway lesion causing ptosis, miosis, and reduced facial sweating on the affected side.
A flexion deformity at the proximal interphalangeal joint of a lesser toe, often related to tight footwear.
An X-linked lysosomal storage disorder with coarse facial features, skeletal abnormalities, and no corneal clouding.
Yellow discoloration of skin and sclera caused by elevated bilirubin, with the pattern helping localize the cause.
A congenital hypogonadotropic hypogonadism associated with absent or reduced sense of smell.
An infusion-related reaction to rapid vancomycin administration causing flushing and itching of the face, neck, and upper torso.
A childhood vasculitis characterized by prolonged fever, conjunctival injection, oral changes, rash, and cervical lymphadenopathy.
A tear of the anteroinferior glenoid labrum associated with recurrent anterior shoulder dislocation.
Inability to extend the wrist and fingers due to radial nerve injury, such as after a humeral shaft fracture.
A nonatherosclerotic inflammatory disease of small and medium arteries strongly associated with tobacco exposure.
A rare lymphoproliferative disorder involving enlarged lymph nodes, with unicentric and multicentric forms.
A dermatophyte infection producing an annular, scaly, expanding rash with central clearing.
A spinal radiographic appearance of fused vertebrae with marginal syndesmophytes, characteristic of ankylosing spondylitis.
An autoimmune pulmonary-renal syndrome characterized by diffuse alveolar hemorrhage and rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis.
An autoimmune cause of hyperthyroidism often associated with diffuse goiter, ophthalmopathy, and pretibial skin changes.
Tiny bluish-white lesions on the buccal mucosa that are a classic early finding of measles.
An abnormality of heart rate or rhythm, which may be too fast, too slow, or irregular, due to disturbed impulse formation or conduction.
A lysosomal storage disease causing progressive neurologic deterioration from psychosine accumulation.
A malignancy of blood-forming tissues causing abnormal proliferation of leukocytes and their precursors.
A tick-borne infection classically associated with an expanding erythema migrans rash and later neurologic, cardiac, or joint disease.
Upward extension of the great toe with fanning of the other toes on stroking the sole; it indicates an upper motor neuron lesion in adults but is normal in infants.
A Plasmodium infection transmitted by Anopheles mosquitoes, classically causing cyclical fevers and hemolysis.
A connective-tissue disorder associated with tall habitus, long limbs and fingers, lens dislocation, and aortic root disease.
Loss of memory, with inability to recall past information or form new memories, which may follow head injury, stroke, or other brain disease.
A highly contagious viral illness with fever, cough, coryza, conjunctivitis, and a descending maculopapular rash.
A recurrent headache disorder often featuring unilateral throbbing pain, nausea, and sensitivity to light or sound.
Periorbital bruising without direct eye trauma, classically suggesting a basilar skull fracture.
A zoonotic orthopoxvirus infection causing fever and characteristic deep-seated vesiculopustular lesions.
A lysosomal lipid-storage disorder that can cause hepatosplenomegaly, neurologic disease, and foam cells.
A neurodegenerative disorder classically producing bradykinesia, resting tremor, rigidity, and postural instability.
Drooping of the upper eyelid, which may arise from third cranial nerve palsy, Horner syndrome, or myasthenia gravis.
A glycogen storage disorder due to acid alpha-glucosidase deficiency, causing hypotonia, cardiomyopathy, or limb-girdle weakness.
Tuberculosis involving the spine, producing vertebral destruction, back pain, and possible paraspinal abscess formation.
A gait in which the hip and knee are lifted high to clear a drooping foot, commonly caused by peroneal nerve palsy.
Primary adrenal insufficiency causing low cortisol and aldosterone, often with hyperpigmentation, hypotension, and electrolyte abnormalities.
A group of inherited neuronal ceroid lipofuscinoses causing progressive neurodegeneration, seizures, and visual loss.
A pupil that does not constrict to light, which may indicate third nerve compression, raised intracranial pressure, or drug effect.
A transient stress-related cardiomyopathy that often causes apical ballooning after intense emotional or physical stress.
An opacity of the crystalline lens causing progressive painless visual blurring and glare.
A fracture of the distal humerus just above the elbow, common in children after a fall on an outstretched arm, with risk to the brachial artery and nerves.
An inherited bone-marrow-failure syndrome with pancytopenia, congenital anomalies, and increased cancer risk.
Tissue necrosis associated with ischemia or severe infection, sometimes producing black discoloration and a foul odor.
A stiff gait in which the legs cross at the knees because of spastic adductor tone, classically seen in cerebral palsy.
Episodic vasospasm of small arteries, usually in fingers or toes, causing sequential pallor, cyanosis, and erythema with cold or stress.
A rare disorder of phytanic-acid accumulation causing retinitis pigmentosa, anosmia, peripheral neuropathy, and cerebellar ataxia.
A drop in blood pressure of at least 20 mmHg systolic or 10 mmHg diastolic within 3 minutes of standing, causing dizziness or fainting, from volume depletion, medications, or autonomic dysfunction.
A pituitary ACTH-producing adenoma causing endogenous hypercortisolism, often with central obesity, striae, and muscle weakness.
A childhood illness with several days of high fever followed by a sudden rose-pink maculopapular rash as the fever resolves.
Abdominal pain that is worse when pressure is suddenly released, suggesting peritoneal irritation such as in appendicitis.
Postpartum pituitary ischemic necrosis causing failure of lactation and multiple anterior pituitary hormone deficiencies.
An intestinal cestode infection acquired by eating undercooked infected meat or food contaminated with eggs, with segments or eggs sometimes found in stool.
Paralysis of a single limb, often from a cortical lesion or a peripheral nerve or plexus injury.
A toxin-mediated neurologic illness causing trismus, muscle rigidity, and painful spasms after contamination of a wound.
An airborne infection caused by an acid-fast bacillus, classically affecting the lungs with chronic cough, fever, weight loss, and night sweats.
An exaggerated fall in systolic blood pressure of more than 10 mmHg during inspiration, classically seen in cardiac tamponade and severe asthma.
A chromosomal disorder caused by an extra chromosome 21, associated with characteristic facial features, hypotonia, and variable intellectual disability.
A monosomy X disorder associated with short stature, gonadal dysgenesis, and characteristic features such as webbed neck.
Thin nails with a concave, spoon-shaped dip, classically linked to iron-deficiency anemia.
A severe form of leptospirosis marked by jaundice and acute kidney injury, often after exposure to water contaminated with animal urine.
A collection of blood between the dura and arachnoid from torn bridging veins, appearing crescent-shaped on CT, especially after head trauma in older adults.
A pre-excitation syndrome caused by an accessory atrioventricular pathway, producing a short PR interval and delta wave on ECG.
A mosquito-borne flaviviral illness that can cause fever, jaundice, hemorrhage, and severe hepatic injury.
A forceful pulse with a rapid upstroke and sudden collapse, with wide pulse pressure, classically seen in aortic regurgitation.
A tick-borne rickettsial illness characterized by fever and a petechial or maculopapular rash that often involves wrists and ankles.
A hand deformity with hyperextended metacarpophalangeal joints and flexed interphalangeal joints of the ring and little fingers, from ulnar nerve injury.
Seeing two images of a single object instead of one; when it disappears on covering either eye, it suggests eye misalignment, as in cranial nerve palsy or myasthenia gravis.
